reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: The eustachian tube stays abnormally open at rest instead of remaining closed and opening only briefly on swallowing or yawning
The cardinal symptom is autophony - patients hear their own voice, and often their own breathing, unnaturally loudly in the affected ear
Breathing-synchronous tinnitus or aural fullness that fluctuates with the respiratory cycle is characteristic
Symptoms typically improve or resolve on lying down, bending forward, or lowering the head, as venous engorgement of the tubal mucosa closes the lumen, and worsen when upright or after exertion
Strongly associated with weight loss, including rapid loss from illness, bariatric surgery, or GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, as well as dehydration, pregnancy, and oestrogen use
Otoscopy may show a tympanic membrane that moves medially and laterally with respiration, and tympanometry can demonstrate pressure swings synchronous with breathing

Reassurance and explanation are the mainstay, as the condition is benign and often self-limiting; correcting dehydration or weight loss and using measures to plump the tubal lining help selected patients
It is frequently mistaken for obstructive eustachian tube dysfunction, and inappropriate ventilation-tube insertion can make the autophony worse
reference.pathophysiology: The eustachian tube is normally closed at rest, opening momentarily during swallowing or yawning to equalise middle-ear pressure. In a patulous tube the lumen remains open, so sound and airflow from the nasopharynx pass directly into the middle ear, producing autophony and breathing-synchronous symptoms. The usual mechanism is loss of the peritubal soft-tissue and mucosal bulk that normally keeps the tube collapsed, as occurs with weight loss, dehydration, or reduction of the fat around Ostmann's pad. Lying down or lowering the head increases venous congestion of the tubal mucosa, which closes the lumen and relieves symptoms, accounting for the strongly positional pattern.
additionalInvestigations: Tympanometry during quiet and forced respiration to detect breathing-related pressure swings
Pure-tone audiometry to exclude other causes of aural symptoms
Nasoendoscopy of the eustachian tube orifice
Otoscopy observing tympanic membrane movement synchronous with breathing
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to exclude superior canal dehiscence
Nutritional and weight assessment, including recent weight loss or GLP-1 agonist use
redFlags: Persistently unilateral symptoms with a possible nasopharyngeal mass, requiring exclusion of tumour
Rapidly progressive or profound hearing loss
Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo suggesting superior canal dehiscence rather than a patulous tube
reference.prognosis: Often benign and self-limiting, especially when a reversible precipitant such as dehydration or recent weight loss is corrected; a minority have persistent troublesome autophony that may require procedural intervention.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as obstructive eustachian tube dysfunction and inserting a ventilation tube, which usually fails and can worsen autophony
Overlooking recent weight loss, GLP-1 agonist use, or dehydration as the trigger
Not recognising the improvement on lying down as a key diagnostic clue
Missing a nasopharyngeal lesion in a persistently unilateral case
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Correct reversible precipitants first by rehydrating, encouraging restoration of lost weight, and reviewing causative oestrogen or GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy
Reassure and advise positional manoeuvres such as lowering the head, which engorge the tubal mucosa and relieve autophony
Trial topical measures that bulk or irritate the tubal mucosa, such as nasal saline or oestrogen or irritant nasal drops
Consider procedural intervention for persistent troublesome autophony, including peritubal injection augmentation of the tubal orifice or eustachian tube obliteration
Insert a ventilation tube in selected patients, recognising the response is variable
Refer to otolaryngology when symptoms persist despite conservative measures and exclude mimics such as superior canal dehiscence
